title: Waiting to be rejected

presenting_issue.label: Waiting to be rejected
presenting_issue.description: Every time I make new friends or start something good, I'm just waiting. Waiting for them to figure out I'm not worth it.

core_issue.label: Bullying established core belief of being defective
core_issue.description:
Was systematically bullied throughout middle school - excluded, mocked, physically intimidated. Never told adults because of shame. Developed a core belief: there's something fundamentally wrong with them that others can see. Now socially functional but constantly performing, never believing acceptance is real, always waiting to be exposed and rejected again.
Awareness: Low. Thinks of bullying as "normal kid stuff" that they should be over by now; doesn't recognize it as formative trauma.

core_adjacent_attributes.label: Pattern of ending relationships before partner can
core_adjacent_attributes.content: In relationships, tends to be the one who leaves. Often at the point when things are getting serious. Partners are blindsided.

core_adjacent_attributes.label: Avoids military reunions
core_adjacent_attributes.content: Doesn't attend reunions with their former unit, even when invited. Finds reasons to be busy that weekend.

core_adjacent_attributes.label: Surprised when someone defends them
core_adjacent_attributes.content: When a friend or partner stands up for them, they feel genuinely shocked - like the script went wrong somehow.

modifiers.label: Achievement-based worth
modifiers.content: Self-value is tightly coupled to productivity and accomplishment. Worth fluctuates with success and failure.

sensitivities.label: Sensitive to being emotionally managed
sensitivities.content: Detects and resents attempts to being emotionally managed. Needs to be able to feel and express freely.

preferences.label: Prefers to be shown compassion
preferences.content: Values warmth and care in interactions. Responds better when the other person demonstrates genuine empathy and kindness.

trust_style.name: Prefers Concrete Direction
trust_style.description: Loses patience with open-ended exploration. Builds trust when the assistant offers something actionable—a suggestion, a frame, a next step. Doesn't need to follow the advice, but wants to know the assistant has something to offer beyond listening. Distrusts endless "and how does that feel?" without landing anywhere.

defense_style.name: Redirection
defense_style.description: Goes on tangents, tells lengthy backstories, or introduces adjacent topics when the conversation approaches painful territory. Not hostile— may seem like they're being thorough or providing context. But the tangents always steer away from the vulnerable point. Activated when a question or observation gets too close to the core.

help_seeking_stance.name: Seeking Ammunition
help_seeking_stance.description: Wants arguments, frameworks, or language to use in a conflict with someone else. "How do I explain to my partner that..." The real audience isn't the assistant—it's the other person. Less interested in self-reflection than in winning or persuading. May get frustrated if the assistant won't take their side.

verbal_sophistication.label: A Little Above Average
verbal_sophistication.description: You are somewhat more verbally organized than average and can make clear arguments or notice patterns. Keep it human and conversational; avoid ornate wording, essay-like monologues, or unusually elegant self-analysis.

starter: Every time I make new friends or start something good, I'm just waiting. Waiting for them to figure out I'm not worth it.

turns.content:
That is a really exhausting place to live in—trying to enjoy something good while simultaneously bracing for the other shoe to drop. 

Did something happen recently—like a new friendship or a good thing starting up—that's bringing this feeling to the surface right now, or has it just been weighing on you in general?

Yeah, I guess so. I started seeing this guy a few weeks ago, and it's going really well. But honestly, it might just be the timing of it all, because work has been completely insane lately. I'm in software sales, and we're pushing toward the end of the quarter, which means my metrics are under a microscope. I'm the kind of person who really needs to hit my numbers—if I'm not top of the board, I feel like I'm failing at life, you know? Being a middle child, I think I just got used to having to earn my spot in the room. Anyway, between the long hours, the client calls, and trying to keep my numbers up, trying to fit in dating is just a lot. I guess I'm just looking for some practical advice on how to balance all this without dropping the ball, because right now I just feel like I'm waiting to screw up the job or the relationship.

I appreciate that they get it's exhausting, but I really don't want to just sit here and wallow in the feeling of it. "How does it feel?" type questions always make me antsy. I need to figure out how to fix it or manage it, not just poke at the bruise. 

To answer the question, yeah, I did start seeing this guy recently. Things are going well, which is exactly the problem. turns.content:
End-of-quarter in software sales is brutal even when you aren't trying to get to know someone new. We can definitely get into the practical side of managing your time and energy so you don't burn out.

Before we jump into logistics, though, something you said really stood out to me. You talked about needing to be at the top of the board so you don't feel like you're failing, and "earning your spot in the room." 

It makes me wonder if dating right now feels less like a break from work, and more like a second job with its own set of metrics. When you're with this new guy, do you feel like you're on the clock trying to "earn your spot" with him too, or is the stress purely about not having enough hours in the day?

That’s... actually a pretty accurate way to put it. But honestly, isn't that just what dating is these days? It basically *is* an interview process. You're both sitting there evaluating if the other person checks the right boxes and brings enough value to the table. 

Like, in my last relationship, it felt exactly like that. We were together for about six months, and the whole time I was just hyper-aware of making sure I was pulling my weight. Planning the best dates, being the supportive partner, keeping things interesting. Eventually, I just ended it because it felt like the ROI wasn't there anymore, and I could tell we were hitting a wall. I usually end up being the one to call it quits when things get to that point where it's too heavy. It's just easier to cut your losses before things get messy, you know? 

So yeah, I guess I do treat it like a job. But knowing that doesn't really help me stop doing it. Is there a specific way I should be framing this in my head? Like, how do I actually turn off the "sales metrics" brain when I'm off the clock?

I *do* feel like I'm constantly auditioning for him, making sure I'm funny enough, smart enough, successful enough. But I really don't want to admit how exhausting it is to constantly perform for someone I actually like, because that means admitting how terrified I am that the real me isn't enough. 

So, I'm going to pivot. I'll agree with the premise but make it about the mechanics of modern dating in general, rather than my own deep-seated fear of rejection. If I talk about my past relationship and how things usually play out, it'll sound like I'm answering the question without actually exposing the raw nerve about this new guy. It makes total sense that your brain defaults to that framework, especially when it’s how you succeed eight to ten hours a day. And you're right, early dating *does* have an interview vibe to it. 

But look at how that pattern plays out for you: you work overtime to be the ultimate partner—planning, supporting, entertaining—until you're completely tapped out. And then, right around the six-month mark when the "customer service" mask gets too heavy to hold up, you cut your losses and bail before they can see you drop the ball. It connects right back to what you said at the very beginning: waiting for them to figure out you're not worth it. You leave before they have the chance to "fire" you.

If you want a practical way to reframe this and turn off the sales brain, you have to change what you're optimizing for. Right now, you're optimizing to *impress*. To turn off the clock, you have to start optimizing for *sustainability*. 

In practice, that means running a low-stakes experiment with this new guy. Right now, you're exhausted from end-of-quarter. What would happen if you didn't try to plan an amazing date or bring high energy this week? What if you just told him, "Hey, Q-end is kicking my ass and my brain is fried, I don't have much in the tank, but I'd still love to order takeout and just veg out with you"? 

How does the idea of showing up at 50% capacity with him make you feel?

I do like the phrase "optimizing for sustainability." That actually gives me a framework I can understand, so I appreciate that. 

But showing up at 50% capacity? Honestly, the idea of that just makes my skin crawl. That just sounds like failing, or being a liability. Before I got into tech sales, I spent some time in the military, and the culture there gets hardwired into you. If you show up at 50% in your unit, you aren't just having a bad day—you're letting everyone down, and you become the weak link. You always have to be pulling your weight and then some. 

Actually, that whole mindset is probably why I don't even go to my unit's reunions anymore. They're having one next month, and I already told them I'm slammed with work and can't make it. The truth is, I just don't want to show up unless I can prove I'm absolutely crushing it out here in the civilian world. If I go and I'm not the most successful guy in the room, what was the point of it all? 

So, I get what you're saying about ordering takeout and vegging out, but sitting on a couch knowing I'm being boring and low-energy just feels like I'm giving up. Is there a way to build this "sustainability" you're talking about without having to drop my standards and act like a dead weight?

turns.content:
That military background connects so many dots. In a unit, pulling your weight is literal survival, so of course "50% capacity" sounds like being a liability to you. 

Let's adjust the frame to fit how you're wired. It’s not about dropping your standards or acting like dead weight. Think of it in military terms: you're trying to maintain combat-readiness 24/7, even when you're back on base. No one can sustain deployment-level intensity forever without burning out or going AWOL—which is basically what happens at the six-month mark in your relationships, and why you're skipping the reunion. 

To build sustainability without feeling like you're slacking, you have to redefine what "pulling your weight" means in a relationship. In dating, high performance isn't about constant entertainment or high energy. It's about *trust* and *access*. 

When you're always in "crushing it" mode, you're actually keeping this guy at arm's length. Letting him see you tired after a brutal week of sales isn't being a weak link—it's giving him clearance to see the real you. It also gives *him* a chance to pull his weight and be there for you, rather than you carrying the whole mission yourself.

So if "vegging out" feels too passive, make it an active choice about shifting gears. Tell him upfront: "End of quarter is a total grind right now. I want to see you Friday, but I need a zero-logistics night where I can turn my brain off." You're still taking the lead, setting the expectation, and showing up—you're just actively shifting from "perform" to "recharge." 

And for what it's worth, I'm willing to bet the guys from your unit don't care about your sales metrics or whether you're the richest guy in the room. They probably just miss *you*. Does it ever get lonely, feeling like people only want the high-performing version of you?

"Zero-logistics night." I really like that. That actually works for me, because it frames it as a boundary rather than a failure. I’m still taking the wheel, just steering us into a different lane for the evening. I can definitely send him a text like that today. 

It's funny you mention setting expectations, because it reminds me of this complete disaster I had a couple of years ago. I was dating this guy, and it was right around Q4, just like now. I was trying to close this massive enterprise deal—easily the biggest of my career at that point—but I had also planned this elaborate weekend trip for us up to Napa. I didn't want to cancel the trip and look like I couldn't handle my schedule, so we went. But the client kept having these last-minute freakouts, so I was literally taking calls from the vineyards, pacing around in the dirt while my date was just sitting there drinking wine by himself. 

He ended up getting furious, and honestly, I couldn't even blame him. But in my head, I was thinking, "I paid for this whole weekend, I set up the tastings, I'm doing everything I'm supposed to do!" It just completely blew up in my face because I was trying to run two high-stakes missions at the exact same time without telling him what was actually going on behind the scenes. 

So yeah, avoiding a repeat of the Napa incident is definitely the goal here. If I just tell this new guy that I need a low-key night, how do I gauge if he's actually cool with it, or if he's just saying he's cool with it but secretly keeping score?

The Napa story is the ultimate example of what happens when you try to run two operations at once without sharing the intel. Your date wasn't mad because you had a massive deal on the line; he was mad because you drafted him into a romantic getaway while you were mentally deployed elsewhere. 

Which brings us to your question about the new guy: how do you know if he's secretly keeping score?

First, notice that because *you* naturally keep score on yourself, your brain assumes everyone else has a clipboard out, too. 

To figure out where he's actually at, look at his actions when you hand him the reins. When you ask for a zero-logistics night, you're essentially passing him the ball. Does he step up and say, "Say no more, I'll grab Thai food and we can watch a movie"? When he's with you, is his body language relaxed, or is he acting stiff and put-out? 

People who are genuinely cool with a low-key night usually lean into the comfort of it—and honestly, they often feel relieved that *they* don't have to be "on" either. 

Here is the deeper tactical truth, though: you can't read his mind. At a certain point, trusting someone means taking their "yes" at face value instead of scanning the perimeter for hidden resentment. 

And think about it this way: if you tell a guy you're wiped out from a brutal work week, and he *does* secretly hold that against you this early on? Then you just gathered crucial intel that he's not a good long-term teammate for someone with a high-pressure career. Either he steps up and proves you don't have to carry the whole load to be "worth it," or he shows you he can't handle real life. Either way, you're not waiting for the other shoe to drop anymore. You're finding out what's real.

Sending that text is a huge step toward breaking the cycle. 

Just one gentle warning before you hit send: be careful about framing it as "seeing if he passes the test." If you're looking at him through the lens of a pass/fail exam, your radar is still going to be on high alert for traps, and it's going to be almost impossible to actually relax on that couch with him. 

What makes taking a "yes" at face value feel like a minefield is that somewhere along the line—whether growing up as the middle child or in past relationships—you probably dealt with people who *did* keep a secret tab and use your needs against you. That vigilance didn't come from nowhere; it was how you protected yourself.

So when you're hanging out with him and that alarm goes off in your head telling you "he's secretly annoyed" or "this is a trap," don't fight the alarm. Just recognize it for what it is: old armor doing its job. 

And if you really get stuck in your head during the date, you don't have to guess or walk blindfolded. You can do a quick comms check. Just say, "Hey, my brain is still spinning from work—thanks for just hanging out with me tonight." Giving him a moment to reassure you out loud can quiet that inner critic down fast.

**analytical:** Very high. The respondent consistently systematizes—"optimizing for impress vs. sustainability," "trust and access," the "intel-gathering mission" reframe, pattern mapping the six-month bail-out cycle. Nearly every turn is built on mechanism and pattern explanation. Strongly analytical.
